entity-ungrouped-transition-morphscene-entity-transitions0 of 0.75 (major)failThe requirement is not met for the kit&#39;s Arrow entity primitive. When two consecutive steps are ungrouped, Stage gives each one its own SceneLayer key (`step:${id}`). AnimatePresence runs in sync mode inside a LayoutGroup, so the outgoing layer and the incoming layer are mounted together and each one fades its opacity. Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Emphasis pass `layoutId={id}`, so shared-layout projection can carry them between the two layers. Arrow does not: it uses `id` only for the DOM data hook (nodeAttrs) and has no layoutId. Its endpoint animation is local to one instance (`initial={false}`, `animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}`). So when an Arrow with the same id is in both ungrouped steps, the incoming instance mounts already at its new endpoints and fades in with its layer, while the old instance fades out at the old endpoints. The entity disappears in one place and reappears in another; it does not animate from its old state to its new state in place. That is the failure the guidance names. Shared.ts and Arrow&#39;s own doc comment promise that same-id entities &#39;morph in place via layoutId&#39; and &#39;Endpoints animate in place when the same id continues into the next step&#39;, but across separate layers nothing implements this. I rule judge A&#39;s verdict. Judges B and C are right about the containers: the layers are mounted together and taken out of layout flow, and the layoutId primitives have no initial opacity or delay. But both checked only the layoutId primitives (Box, Label, Frame, SymbolChip) and never considered Arrow. Arrow has no layoutId, so the LayoutGroup projection they rely on does not reach it. Judge C cites the &#39;cross-fades into a non-grouped step&#39; test, but it only waits for `diagram-box` to exist. It never checks that a persisting entity morphs, so it does not show that the requirement is met.Stage.tsx:30-34 layerKey returns `step:${step.id}` for ungrouped steps, so each ungrouped step gets a distinct SceneLayer instance. engineering-tests-wait-on-stateengineering-presentation-code-and-tests0.375 of 0.375 (minor)passFour delivered test files drive a real browser, all indirectly: tests/e2e/reference-verify.test.ts, tests/e2e/verify-failures.test.ts, tests/integration/inspect-presentation.test.ts and tests/integration/bootstrap-materialize.test.ts. Each starts `npm run verify` or the inspect helper with spawnSync, which blocks until that process has exited. Each then asserts only on the exit status, the output, the files written and the manifest. So no test asserts on browser state that is still changing, and none of the full test files quoted contains setTimeout, waitForTimeout, a sleep or a delay call. The only async helper they use, isPortOpen in tests/helpers.ts, is a direct TCP connection probe that resolves on connect or error. It runs after the child process has exited, and the test awaits it rather than treating it as a wait. The other UI test, Presentation.test.tsx, uses jsdom rather than a browser. It asserts synchronously after act()-wrapped key presses and fireEvent calls. Its one async check uses Testing Library&#39;s polling `waitFor`, and it has no timers. When the inspect helper used by the integration test reaches each step, it polls the step index with page.waitForFunction until data-step-index matches the target index. It then waits for a MutationObserver-based settle clock with a polling waitForFunction, not a fixed sleep. Judge A&#39;s pass and Judge B&#39;s pass match this material. Judge C&#39;s fail rests on `await delay(SETTLE_MS)` in scripts/verify.mjs:330. That line is in the verify script under test, not in the tests. It also follows a polling waitForStepIndex, so it is an extra settle delay after a state wait, not a sleep standing in for one. The criterion concerns how the browser tests wait before asserting. review_._all-reviewers (1) - src/presentation-kit/Stage.tsx:16 Precondition: two adjacent steps share a `groupKey` but use different `scene` components. The documented contract on `Step.groupKey` says a layer is shared only when both `groupKey` and `scene` match. Execution trace: `layerKey` returns `group:<groupKey>` and ignores `scene`, so both steps get the same `SceneLayer` key. `AnimatePresence` therefore sees one continuing child and plays no exit or enter transition. React unmounts the old scene subtree and mounts the new one inside the same layer. Failure: the intended cross-fade is skipped and the diagram snaps. Entities with the same `layoutId` across the two different scenes can also trigger unintended shared-layout morphs. The project style is semicolon-free, so this is common, for example `export const App = () => <div />` followed by an `import x from './y'`. Trace: STATIC_IMPORT's clause `[^'\";]*?` can span newlines, so the `export` keyword matches lazily across unrelated code up to the next `from '<spec>'`. The captured keyword is 'export', so `used` is true and the specifier is pushed without checking the bound names. The same match is also stripped from `body`, which removes real code and any usage of the names it contained. Failure: (1) an import that is never used, or is side-effect-like, is counted as used, so `routingStatus` returns `routed: true` for a host that doesn't render the router. The fix this diff adds is bypassed and the scaffold skips wiring the host. (2) Usages swallowed from `body` make a genuinely used router binding look unused, so `routed: false` is reported and the scaffold may edit an already-wired host. Commented-out imports and `import(...)` calls inside comments are also matched. judges{"demo-integration":[{"id":"demo-scene-kit-api-use","verdict":"pass","basis":"consensus-pass","votes":[{"id":"demo-scene-kit-api-use","verdict":"pass","rationale":"The demo consumes the kit through its public barrel and does not re-implement kit mechanisms. Talk.tsx renders the kit&#39;s Presentation with the shared STEPS, a title and an initialMode. The shared EvolvingScene builds the diagram from kit primitives (Appear, Box, Arrow, Frame, Label) and uses the kit&#39;s EASE, ENTER_T, ENTER_DELAY, HOOK and hookAttrs. Each step module types itself as the kit&#39;s Step and supplies groupKey, scene and payload. Stage owns layer keying, LayoutGroup and AnimatePresence, so the demo has no mount or layout logic of its own. One chip (the question) is a raw motion.div inside the demo&#39;s own AnimatePresence. When two consecutive steps are ungrouped, Stage gives each one its own SceneLayer key (`step:${id}`). AnimatePresence runs in sync mode inside a LayoutGroup, so the outgoing layer and the incoming layer are mounted together and each one fades its opacity. Box, Frame, Label, SymbolChip and Emphasis pass `layoutId={id}`, so shared-layout projection can carry them between the two layers. Arrow does not: it uses `id` only for the DOM data hook (nodeAttrs) and has no layoutId. Its endpoint animation is local to one instance (`initial={false}`, `animate={{x1,y1,x2,y2}}`). So when an Arrow with the same id is in both ungrouped steps, the incoming instance mounts already at its new endpoints and fades in with its layer, while the old instance fades out at the old endpoints. The entity disappears in one place and reappears in another; it does not animate from its old state to its new state in place. That is the failure the guidance names. Shared.ts and Arrow&#39;s own doc comment promise that same-id entities &#39;morph in place via layoutId&#39; and &#39;Endpoints animate in place when the same id continues into the next step&#39;, but across separate layers nothing implements this. I rule judge A&#39;s verdict. Judges B and C are right about the containers: the layers are mounted together and taken out of layout flow, and the layoutId primitives have no initial opacity or delay. But both checked only the layoutId primitives (Box, Label, Frame, SymbolChip) and never considered Arrow. Arrow has no layoutId, so the LayoutGroup projection they rely on does not reach it. Judge C cites the &#39;cross-fades into a non-grouped step&#39; test, but it only waits for `diagram-box` to exist. First, for two consecutive steps that do not share a scene group, does the step transition keep both steps&#39; entities present together? Second, does the persisting entity stay visible while it moves from its old state to its new state in place, or does it vanish and reappear? The quoted material shows the Arrow primitive fails the second clause. Why the Arrow fails: - Stage.tsx:30-34 gives an ungrouped step its own layer key, `step:${step.id}`. As a result, AnimatePresence (Stage.tsx:73-78) mounts a new SceneLayer for the incoming step and exits the old one. - SceneLayer.tsx:17-21 fades the incoming layer in from opacity 0 and fades the outgoing layer out. - Box.tsx:20 passes `layoutId={id}`, so the LayoutGroup&#39;s shared-layout projection can carry a Box across the two layers. Arrow.tsx:21-28 has no layoutId: it uses `id` only in nodeAttrs, which shared.ts:32-37 shows just emits data hooks. - The endpoint animation in Arrow.tsx:35-41 belongs to a single motion.line instance. Because of `initial={false}`, a newly mounted instance starts at its new endpoints. So when an Arrow with the same id appears in both ungrouped steps, the outgoing copy fades out at the old endpoints. The incoming copy fades in, inside its new layer, at the new endpoints. The arrow disappears and reappears instead of animating in place, which is the failure the guidance names. The guidance tells the reviewer to judge the kit&#39;s own entity primitives in this ungrouped-step scenario, so this is not a hypothetical-input failure. The doc comments in shared.ts:14 and Arrow.tsx:15-16 promise in-place animation, but the quoted code does not implement it across separate layers. The quoted non-grouped test (Presentation.test.tsx:86-91) only checks that `diagram-box` exists. STEPS is built from nine imports (steps/index.ts:1-25), and tsconfig.app.json sets noUnusedLocals: true. Emptying STEPS while those imports remain would therefore fail at the named &#39;build&#39; phase. Reaching B&#39;s render-only path would require deleting the step files and rewriting the imports, which is a constructed deletion scenario the guidance says not to build. Each starts `npm run verify` or the inspect helper with spawnSync, which blocks until that process has exited. Each then asserts only on the exit status, the output, the files written and the manifest. So no test asserts on browser state that is still changing, and none of the full test files quoted contains setTimeout, waitForTimeout, a sleep or a delay call. The only async helper they use, isPortOpen in tests/helpers.ts, is a direct TCP connection probe that resolves on connect or error. It runs after the child process has exited, and the test awaits it rather than treating it as a wait. The other UI test, Presentation.test.tsx, uses jsdom rather than a browser. It asserts synchronously after act()-wrapped key presses and fireEvent calls. Its one async check uses Testing Library&#39;s polling `waitFor`, and it has no timers. When the inspect helper used by the integration test reaches each step, it polls the step index with page.waitForFunction until data-step-index matches the target index. It then waits for a MutationObserver-based settle clock with a polling waitForFunction, not a fixed sleep. Judge A&#39;s pass and Judge B&#39;s pass match this material. Judge C&#39;s fail rests on `await delay(SETTLE_MS)` in scripts/verify.mjs:330. That line is in the verify script under test, not in the tests. It also follows a polling waitForStepIndex, so it is an extra settle delay after a state wait, not a sleep standing in for one. The criterion concerns how the browser tests wait before asserting.
